summary.text: Easy cases use a decimal shift of either \(n\), a power of ten, or \(D(n)\); the only small residual cases are handled by explicit partners. In the general case, writing \(d=D(n)\), \(A\) for the number of digits of \(d\), and \(M=(n-D(d))/9\), the construction \(m=d(10^M-1)10^A+d\) has \(d\mid m\) and \(D(m)=9M+D(d)=n\); appending enough zeros to \(m\) then makes it a distinct partner without changing its digit sum.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(r)\) denote the sum of the base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(r\). For a fixed positive integer \(n\), call \(k\) a partner of \(n\) if
\[
 k>0,\qquad k\ne n,\qquad D(n)\mid k,\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
We prove that every positive \(n\) has such a partner. Since \(a(n)\) is defined to be the least partner when partners exist, and to be \(0\) only when none exist, this will prove \(a(n)\ne0\).

We use several elementary facts about decimal digits.

1. If \(r>0\), then \(D(r)>0\).

2. Appending zeros does not change digit sum: for \(p\ge0\) and \(r>0\),
\[
D(10^p r)=D(r).
\]

3. Every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its digit sum. Thus
\[
r\equiv D(r)\pmod 9.
\]

4. If \(\ell(r)\) is the number of decimal digits of \(r\) (with \(\ell(0)=0\)), then
\[
D(r)\le 9\ell(r).
\]
Also, \(\ell(r)\le t\) is equivalent to \(r<10^t\). In particular, if \(r>0\) and \(L=\ell(r)\), then
\[
10^{L-1}\le r<10^L.
\]

5. For every \(t\ge0\), \(t\le10^t\). This follows by induction: it is clear for \(t=0\), and if \(t\le10^t\), then \(t+1\le10^t+1\le10^{t+1}\).

We first record some simple ways to manufacture a partner.

If \(D(n)\mid n\), then \(k=10n\) is a partner. Indeed, \(k>n\), so \(k\ne n\), and \(D(k)=D(n)\). Hence \(D(n)\mid k\) and \(D(k)=D(n)\mid n\).

Next, suppose \(D(n)\mid10^p\) for some \(p\). Put
\[
T=p+n+1,\qquad k=10^T.
\]
Because \(T\ge p\), \(10^p\mid10^T\), so \(D(n)\mid k\). Moreover, \(D(k)=1\), which divides \(n\). Finally,
\[
k=10^T\ge T>n,
\]
so \(k\) is positive and distinct from \(n\).

A third construction applies when
\[
D(D(n))\mid n.
\]
Write \(d=D(n)\), and set
\[
k=d\,10^{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d>0\), so \(k>0\), and
\[
k\ge10^{n+1}\ge n+1>n.
\]
Clearly \(d=D(n)\mid k\), while appending zeros gives
\[
D(k)=D(d)=D(D(n))\mid n.
\]
Thus \(k\) is again a partner.

We shall also use a shifted version of any auxiliary solution. Suppose \(m>0\) satisfies
\[
D(n)\mid m\quad\hbox{and}\quad D(m)\mid n.
\]
Then
\[
k=10^{n+1}m
\]
is a partner of \(n\). Indeed, \(D(k)=D(m)\), and \(D(n)\mid m\) implies \(D(n)\mid k\). Also
\[
k\ge10^{n+1}>n,
\]
so distinctness is automatic. Consequently, in what follows it is enough to construct a positive \(m\) with those two divisibility properties; a sufficiently large decimal shift turns it into an actual partner.

We now establish the digit-sum identity used in the general construction.

For every \(M\ge0\),
\[
D(10^M-1)=9M,
\]
because \(10^M-1\) is represented by \(M\) digits, all equal to \(9\) (with the assertion also valid for \(M=0\)). More generally, if \(0\le x<10^M\), then
\[
D(x)+D(10^M-1-x)=9M. \tag{1}
\]
This is the usual digitwise complement identity: write \(x\) in exactly \(M\) decimal places by allowing leading zeros. Subtracting it from the string of \(M\) nines replaces every digit \(c\) by \(9-c\), so the two digits in each position sum to \(9\). Summing over all \(M\) positions gives (1).

It follows that if \(d\ge1\) and
\[
\ell(d-1)\le M, \tag{2}
\]
then
\[
D\bigl(d(10^M-1)\bigr)=9M. \tag{3}
\]
For \(d=1\), this is just the identity for \(10^M-1\). If \(d>1\), condition (2) says \(d-1<10^M\), hence \(d\le10^M\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(10^M-1)
 &=d10^M-d\\
 &=(d-1)10^M+(10^M-d).
\end{aligned}
\]
This decimal expression consists of the digits of \(d-1\), followed by an \(M\)-place block representing \(10^M-d\), padded with leading zeros if necessary. Therefore
\[
D\bigl(d(10^M-1)\bigr)=D(d-1)+D(10^M-d).
\]
Since \(10^M-d=10^M-1-(d-1)\), equation (1), with \(x=d-1\), gives (3).

We now prove the existence of a partner for an arbitrary positive \(n\). Set
\[
d=D(n),\qquad e=D(d).
\]
If any of
\[
d\\mid n,\qquad d\mid10^p\text{ for some }p,\qquad e\mid n
\]
holds, one of the three constructions above applies. We may therefore assume that all three statements fail.

First dispose of the small values. A direct examination of \(1\le n<28\), using the displayed digit sums below, shows that under these three failures only \(15,16,25\) can remain:

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 n & \text{reason it is already covered}\\ \hline
1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 & D(n)=n,\text{ so }D(n)\mid n,\\
10 & D(10)=1\mid10,\\
11 & D(11)=2\mid10,\\
12 & D(12)=3,\ D(3)=3\mid12,\\
13 & D(13)=4\mid100,\\
14 & D(14)=5\mid10,\\
17 & D(17)=8\mid1000,\\
18 & D(18)=9,\ D(9)=9\mid18,\\
19 & D(19)=10\mid10,\\
20 & D(20)=2\mid20,\\
21 & D(21)=3\mid21,\\
22 & D(22)=4\mid100,\\
23 & D(23)=5\mid10,\\
24 & D(24)=6\mid24,\\
26 & D(26)=8\mid1000,\\
27 & D(27)=9\mid27.
\end{array}
\]
For the three exceptions we explicitly produce an auxiliary \(m\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 n&D(n)&m&D(m)\\ \hline
15&6&12&3\\
16&7&35&8\\
25&7&14&5
\end{array}
\]
In each row \(D(n)\mid m\) and \(D(m)\mid n\). Thus shifting \(m\) by a factor \(10^{n+1}\) gives a partner. Hence we may assume from now on that
\[
n\ge28. \tag{4}
\]

Because every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its digit sum,
\[
n\equiv d\equiv e\pmod9.
\]
Also digit sum never exceeds the original positive integer, so
\[
e\le d\le n.
\]
Consequently \(n-e\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(9\). Define
\[
M=\frac{n-e}{9};
\]
then
\[
9M=n-e. \tag{5}
\]
Let
\[
A=\ell(d)
\]
and define
\[
m=d(10^M-1)10^A+d. \tag{6}
\]
The point of this definition is that the final \(d\) in (6) occupies the last \(A\) decimal places, while \(d(10^M-1)\) occupies the places to its left. We will prove
\[
D(m)=n. \tag{7}
\]
Once this is done, the required divisibilities are immediate: equation (6) factors as
\[
m=d\bigl((10^M-1)10^A+1\bigr),
\]
so \(d=D(n)\mid m\), while (7) gives \(D(m)=n\mid n\).

It remains to justify the digit-sum calculation, especially the needed length bound
\[
\ell(d-1)\le M. \tag{8}
\]
We split into two cases.

Suppose first that \(d<100\). Then \(d-1<100=10^2\), so \(\ell(d-1)\le2\). Also \(A=\ell(d)\le2\), and hence
\[
e=D(d)\le9A\le18.
\]
Together with \(n\ge28\), this yields \(n-e\ge10\). But \(n-e\) is divisible by \(9\); a nonnegative multiple of \(9\) that is at least \(10\) is at least \(18\). Thus, by (5), \(M\ge2\), proving (8).

Now suppose \(d\ge100\). Let \(L=\ell(n)\). Since each digit of \(n\) is at most \(9\),
\[
d=D(n)\le9L.
\]
The inequality \(d\ge100\) therefore forces \(L\ge12\).

For every \(L\ge1\),
\[
9L<10^L. \tag{9}
\]
This can be proved by induction: it is immediate for \(L=1\), and multiplication of \(10^L\) by \(10\) more than accommodates the increase of \(9L\) to \(9(L+1)\). From \(d\le9L\) and (9), we get \(d<10^L\), so
\[
A=\ell(d)\le L. \tag{10}
\]
Moreover,
\[
e=D(d)\le9A. \tag{11}
\]

We also need the elementary estimate
\[
18L\le10^{L-1}\qquad(L\ge12). \tag{12}
\]
At \(L=12\) this is immediate, since \(216\le10^{11}\). If it holds for \(L\), then
\(10^L=10\cdot10^{L-1}\) is certainly at least \(18(L+1)\); thus induction proves (12). Because an \(L\)-digit number is at least \(10^{L-1}\), (12) gives
\[
n\ge10^{L-1}\ge18L.
\]
Using (10) and (11),
\[
9A+e\le18A\le18L\le n.
\]
Therefore
\[
9A\le n-e=9M,
\]
and hence \(A\le M\). Since \(d<10^A\), we have \(d-1<10^A\le10^M\), which is exactly (8).

Thus (8) holds in all cases. Formula (3) now gives
\[
D\bigl(d(10^M-1)\bigr)=9M. \tag{13}
\]
We also have \(M\ge2\): in the case \(d<100\) this was already shown, while in the case \(d\ge100\), (8) and \(d-1\ge99\) force \(M\ge2\). Hence \(10^M-1>0\), and because \(d>0\), the high block \(d(10^M-1)\) is positive.

Since \(A=\ell(d)\), equation (6) is precisely the decimal concatenation of the positive integer \(d(10^M-1)\) with the \(A\)-digit block representing \(d\). Therefore digit sums add. By (13), by the definition of \(e\), and by (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(m)
 &=D\bigl(d(10^M-1)\bigr)+D(d)\\
 &=9M+e\\
 &=(n-e)+e=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (7). As noted above, \(d=D(n)\mid m\) and \(D(m)=n\mid n\). The shifted number
\[
k=10^{n+1}m
\]
is therefore positive, exceeds \(n\), satisfies \(D(n)\mid k\), and has
\[
D(k)=D(m)=n\mid n.
\]
So it is a partner of \(n\).

We have proved that the set of partners of every positive integer \(n\) is nonempty. Every element of this set is positive, so its least element is also positive. By the definition of the sequence, \(a(n)\) is this least element whenever the set is nonempty. Consequently
\[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every positive integer }n.}
\]
